item.title: Iran vows to end U.S. naval blockade by 'all available means'
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
What to know about the Iran war today: Iran said Monday it would use "all available means" to counter the U.S. naval blockade of the country's ports, which a foreign ministry official described as "an act of military aggression" against the country.President Trump said in a social media post on Sunday that Iran had "launched more drones and missiles in the last week than at any time" during the nearly-nine-month war , but that the increasing attacks had "done no damage." A media outlet linked to Iran's Houthi allies said Monday that a Saudi attack on Yemen's port city of Hodeida killed four people and wounded 18, as fighting between the Saudi-led coalition and the Houthis continues to intensify. Top Iranian diplomat calls land blockade of Iran "impossible" Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi called a land blockade of Iran "impossible" in comments shared Monday, according to Iranian state media . He also said pushing back against U.S. sanctions "is the duty of the entire country and its people," state media reported. "The best way to counter this pressure is to make those imposing sanctions lose hope of achieving their goals, so they know this tool is ineffective and will remain so," Araghchi said. Qatar's prime minister returns to Washington for Rubio meeting U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio met with Mohammed bin Abdulrahman Al Thani, Qatar's prime minister and foreign minister, in Washington, D.C., on Monday. It was the Qatari official's second visit to Washington in recent weeks, after meeting with President Trump earlier this month. At the time, Mr. Trump had said he didn't see a reason to escalate the Iran war after the midterm elections. Qatar has been a key mediator in indirect talks between the U.S. and Iran to end the conflict, which have stalled. U.S. issues dozens of new sanctions against Iran The U.S. Treasury Department issued new sanctions against a group of Iranian nationals and entities, which it described as front companies and exchange houses, on Monday. A list of two dozen names posted to its website included nine Iranian individuals in addition to businesses based, mainly, in Tehran and Dubai. The Treasury said in a news release that the sanctions came as part of "a sweeping effort to disrupt Iran's global shadow banking networks," which, according to the agency, allow billions to circulate internationally and "provide the regime access to foreign currency despite comprehensive sanctions." "Iran's economy is underwater, and its leaders are panicking," said Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent in a statement. "Iran's shadow banking system is the last financial lifeline of a bankrupt regime. Treasury will continue dismantling these illicit networks until we have buried the head of the snake." Coalition fighting Houthis carried out hundreds of strikes in last few hours, Yemen says The military coalition fighting Houthi rebels in Yemen carried out 647 strikes in the last few hours, the Yemeni government said Monday. The attacks included drone, rocket, field artillery and airstrikes, a government spokesperson said in a social media statement . According to the spokesperson, those strikes "targeted militia positions, gatherings, fortifications and movements" and resulted in the "neutralization" of 122 Houthi commanders and members. More than 50 vehicles and pieces of military equipment were destroyed or disabled, the statement said. In a separate statement, also shared to social media , Houthi military spokesman Brig. Gen. Yahya Saree said the Saudi Air Force had carried out 67 airstrikes and missile attacks in the last 24 hours, and that dozens of civilians were killed or wounded. Saree said the strikes killed and wounded dozens of civilians in targeted areas of Yemen's capital, Sana'a, as well as the governorates of Lahj, Taiz, Hodeidah, Saada and Hajjah. But the Yemeni government blamed the Houthis for a missile attack Monday in Taiz, where, its spokesperson said, two civilians were killed and seven others were injured in the village of Kahlan. Houthis say death toll from Saudi attack has risen to 17 Yemen's Houthi rebels said the death toll from a Saudi attack on the Red Sea port city of Hodeida rose to 17 Monday. The Iran-backed fighters, who control a massive portion of Yemen, including Hodeida, are battling a Saudi-led coalition that supports Yemen's internationally recognized government. Coalition airstrikes on telecommunication facilities killed 17 workers, wounded 11 more and caused the "total destruction" of administrative buildings, staff housing, a mosque and other infrastructure on the compound, the Houthis' telecommunications ministry said. "This has led to the complete destruction of these facilities [and] the disruption of telecommunications and internet services," affecting tens of thousands of people, it said. Houthi military spokesman Brig. Gen. Yahya Saree said in a social media post that another alleged Saudi coalition attack in the Lahj province, in Yemen's southwest, targeted buses and other vehicles. He said there were unspecified casualties. Saudi Arabia did not immediately comment on either of the purported attacks. The coalition said Sunday that it had intercepted a ballistic missile launched at Saudi Arabia's western Red Sea coast. CBS/AFP U.S. discussing training Syrian armed forces, Reuters reports The United States is discussing plans to train Syrian soldiers to conduct demining work, five people familiar with the matter told the Reuters news agency. The plan could see a small number of U.S. troops return to Syria as soon as next year if it is adopted. The proposal is for a multinational training mission – made up of 15 countries including the U.K., France and Saudi Arabia – to focus on demining and ordnance disposal. It would be the first time since 2024 that U.S. troops had trained Syrian counterparts. The U.S. State Department told Reuters that Washington welcomed having a partner in the Syrian capital, President Ahmed al-Sharaa , who is committed to combating the terror group ISIS. U.S. officials would need to do due diligence to screen all prospective Syrian recipients of the training before any funding is dedicated to the prospective project, two of the sources told Reuters. Iranian singer convicted of "outraging public decency" lashed 74 times for performing without hijab An Iranian singer has been lashed 74 times after being convicted of the crime of "outraging public decency" for performing without wearing the hijab head covering that is mandatory for women in the country. Parastoo Ahmadi was lashed Monday over her 2024 live-streamed YouTube concert, according to her attorney, who was quoted by the reformist Iranian newspaper Emtemad. The lawyer told Emtemad that Ahmadi and four members of her production team presented themselves to provincial authorities in the holy city of Qom Monday as required after their sentences were upheld in September by a local criminal court. The criminal court in Qom upheld the convictions for "outraging public decency" citing "immoral" content posted online during Ahmadi's performance in December 2024, which went viral in Iran. In addition to the 74 lashes, Parastoo and eight members of her team were also sentenced to a two-year ban on travel out of the country and a two-year ban on all "artistic activity." Parastoo performed her concert in the Dayr-Gachin Caravanserai - an ancient site along the Silk Road route in Iran. It included themes of nationalism and popular uprising, and saw her openly flout both the Islamic Republic's dress code and a long-standing ban on women singing in public. Netanyahu warns against downplaying "grave threats" facing Israel Benjamin Netanyahu, Israel's now-caretaker prime minister, said Monday that Israel is still facing "serious and grave threats," and he warned of the dangers of downplaying them. He spoke shortly after his domestic political opponent, Gadi Eisenkot, said he saw no immediate threat posed by Iran that would warrant military action before a new Israeli government is formed to oust Netanyahu. "Anyone who belittles or downplays these immediate, serious and grave threats surrounding us does so for political reasons," Netanyahu said at a briefing in Israel's parliament, in which he called for a unity government, as Eisenkot attempts to form a new ruling coalition. CBS/AFP Netanyahu foe trying to form new Israeli government says no "immediate threat" requiring action against Iran Gadi Eisenkot, the Israeli politician trying to form a new government to oust current Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu in the wake of national elections, has said he sees no "immediate threat" from Iran requiring military action. Speaking at a meeting of his party, Yashar, Monday, he said: "I see no direct and immediate threat from Iran today that would require Israel to act before a new government is formed." He added that "the gravest threat Iran poses" comes from its stockpile on enriched uranium: "That is where we need to focus." Netanyahu has appeared keen to go on the offensive against Iran again. Sources familiar with the matter told CBS News last week that Israel and the U.S. were considering a new assault on the country . Eisenkot recently said Netanyahu should not make any big national security decisions in the transition period following Israel's election, in which Netanyahu's bloc lost its majority, and that the now-caretaker prime minister should avoid "dangerous steps that can wait for the swearing in of a new government." Iran seeks $290 billion in damages against the U.S. Iran is due $290 billion from the United States to cover damages inflicted both during, and long before the war launched jointly by the U.S. and Israel almost nine months ago, Iran's judiciary authorities say. Iranian courts have demanded the U.S. pay the sum, a judiciary official said Monday. "We have secured court rulings in domestic courts awarding $290 billion in damages against the Americans," said Hassan Abdolianpour, head of the judiciary's center for lawyers, according to state television. He also said several lawsuits had been filed against Persian Gulf Arab nations for "allowing their territory to be used by America to launch attacks against Iran." According to state TV, the damages cover U.S. actions going back decades. On Monday, state broadcaster IRIB said several U.S.-linked commercial ships had been seized and that part of the compensation owed to Iran would be settled through the seizures, without giving further details. CBS/AFP Lebanon denounces Israeli military official's visit to school in south Lebanese officials have denounced a visit by an Israeli military spokesperson to a school in an Israeli-occupied area of southern Lebanon. As Lebanon marked its independence day on Sunday, the Israeli military's Arabic-language spokesperson Ella Waweya shared a video on social media showing her outside a school in Debl, a Christian village, and then standing in front of a classroom full of children. The village is located inside a wide swath of southern Lebanon that Israel has occupied and declared a "security zone" after the latest war erupted with Hezbollah in March. The zone covers a strip of southern Lebanon along the border and stretches about six miles into Lebanese territory. Debl is among a number of Christian-majority villages near the border where many residents have refused to leave despite Israeli military orders to evacuate. Cut off from the rest of Lebanon, they are largely dependent on humanitarian aid. "During my last visit to south Lebanon, I was amazed by the beauty of the land and the villages which have paid a heavy price due to their exploitation ... by a terrorist organization," Waweya said, referring to the Iran-backed Hezbollah militant group. Lebanese Prime Minister Nawaf Salam denounced Israel for "dragging students into a military and propaganda display." "An occupying power has no right to exploit our children to embellish the image of its occupation or impose its dominance over our people in the south," he added. Hezbollah drew Lebanon into the Middle East war in March with rocket fire at Israel, which responded with massive airstrikes and a ground invasion. Lebanon says Israeli attacks since then have killed more than 4,300 people. CBS/AFP Iran says will use "all available means" to counter U.S. blockade Iran said Monday it would use all means at its disposal to counter a U.S. naval blockade imposed in retaliation for its own push to block the Strait of Hormuz. "We will certainly not tolerate these actions and will use all available means to counter U.S. aggression," foreign ministry spokesman Esmaeil Baqaei said in his weekly press briefing. Soon after the war broke out, the Strait of Hormuz became the focus of the conflict, with Iran continuing in its efforts to blockade the waterway, vital to global energy supplies. In response, the U.S. imposed its own counterblockade of Iranian ports. It later announced a raft of economic sanctions, and launched a task force to disrupt land routes into Iran. "You should bear in mind that what the Americans have described as economic sanctions, an economic blockade and a naval blockade undoubtedly constitutes an act of military aggression against Iran," said Baqaei. "Under these circumstances, Iran is entitled, pursuant to Article 51 of the U.N. Charter, to use any means at its disposal to defend itself." Iran has said Hormuz could be open within two days but only if Washington agreed to its list of demands , which include the lifting of the blockade. Houthi media say 4 dead in Saudi attack on key port city Houthi media said Monday that a Saudi attack killed four people and wounded 18 in Yemen's key port city of Hodeida. The Iran-backed fighters, who control large swathes of Yemen including Hodeida, are battling a Saudi-led coalition that backs Yemen's internationally recognized government. The strike targeted a building belonging to Yemen's Public Telecommunications Corporation, the Houthis' Almasirah television channel wrote on X. Riyadh didn't immediately comment on the report. It came a day after the Saudi-led coalition said it had intercepted a ballistic missile launched toward the kingdom's western Red Sea coast. That region is home to major oil installations that Houthi fighters have attacked in recent weeks, along with strikes on airports and military sites. Yemen, which has been embroiled in more than a decade of civil war, was sucked into the U.S.-Iran conflict in July when a truce between the Houthis and the Saudi-backed government unraveled. Since then, hostilities have left more than 1,600 people dead and more than 300,000 displaced in the country, the poorest on the Arabian Peninsula, according to the latest U.N. data. Houthis say Saudi strike on Yemen capital wounds 6 Houthi rebels in Yemen reported an airstrike early Sunday in the capital, Sanaa. A spokesperson for the Houthi-run Health Ministry, Anees al-Asbahi, said the strike hit a fuel station operated by the state-run oil company and wounded six workers. The strike also damaged the company's building, al-Asbahi said. The Red Sea port city of Mokha also came under fire on Sunday, Houthi-run television reported, as did the Haifan district in the southwestern province of Taiza. The Houthis blamed Saudi Arabia for the airstrikes but didn't report any casualties from them. Trump says Iran launched more drones and missiles in past week "than at any time for over a year" President Trump on Sunday acknowledged that Iran "has launched more drones and missiles in the last week than at any time for over a year," but he added: "Don't worry, they've all been knocked down, and done no damage." In a post on Truth Social, the president linked the midterm elections — in which Democrats won majorities in both chambers of Congress — to the escalation in the war with Iran. "As everyone remembers, I predicted two things concerning the November 3rd Midterm Elections. One, that if the Democrats win, the Stock Markets would go down, substantially, which they have, and two, that the Islamic Republic of Iran, which has killed 81,000 protestors as of today, will grow more aggressive in their attacks, which has also occurred," Mr. Trump said. Higher fuel prices triggered by the war caused economic concerns for Americans, and top Republicans, including Vice President JD Vance, have partly attributed GOP election defeats to the war with Iran. Mr. Trump on Sunday said voters "didn't understand" what their votes meant and called the election "very 'strange.'" "Iranian leaders consider the Democrats weak, ineffective, and Country destroying, but I won't let that happen! Both the Dems and Iran fought like hell to keep the Oil price up as long as possible and, since the Election, the Oil price has dropped by a record level," he said. "Too bad the Voters didn't understand this before they pulled the trigger, but the whole Election was very 'strange.'" Athlete swims Strait of Hormuz to raise awareness of Iran war's toll on wildlife British endurance swimmer Lewis Pugh has swum in the North Pole and Antarctica to draw attention to environmental causes. But battling freezing waters and extreme conditions hasn't prepared him for his latest challenge: swimming the Strait of Hormuz while tankers are attacked and blown up nearby. Pugh, who is a United Nations Patron of the Oceans, spent three days this week swimming parts of the dangerous waterway to highlight how the war with Iran threatens the area's habitat and wildlife. Wearing only swimming trunks, goggles and a cap bearing the U.N. logo, the athlete started from the Musandam Peninsula, on the southern tip of the strait, and ended by rounding the Cape of Hormuz, completing about 9.3 miles in total. Pugh is believed to be the first person to undertake a long-distance swim there since the war started. The swimmer said that minutes after he entered the water on Monday, he heard two loud explosions that rocked the sea. Read more here . Iran holds talks with Qatari mediators Iranian deputy foreign minister Kazem Gharibabadi said on Saturday that a Qatari delegation visited Tehran the previous evening and "held two hours of talks," without providing details. Negotiations between the U.S. and Iran to end the war have stalled in recent months. Iran's Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said, however, that ongoing talks in the region must be "given a chance" and that the ongoing U.S. blockade of the Strait of Hormuz "must be lifted rationally." "Our position is clear: as long as Iran's demands are not met, the discussion on the Strait of Hormuz and its opening is pointless," he said, quoted by state television. "At the same time, we have always affirmed our readiness for dialogue, just as we are ready to defend ourselves." Iran's conditions have included ending the war on all fronts, unfreezing Iranian assets, lifting oil sanctions and ending the U.S. counter-blockade of Iranian ports. CBS/AFP Trump says he wants to make "permanent" deal with Iranian regime President Trump said Saturday that he wants to make a "permanent" deal with Iran that will prevent the country from gaining a nuclear weapon in the future. "What I'm doing is I'm going to make it so that if we have an incompetent president in four years or 15 years or 20 years, I'm going to make a deal that is going to be permanent," Mr. Trump told Fox News in a phone interview on Saturday. "I'm not going to let somebody allow them to have a nuclear weapon." Mr. Trump said he's never "cared too much about the regime" leading Iran, and that he has "taken out two regimes already," though he declined to specify further. Former Supreme Leader Ali Khamenei was killed in the initial strikes on Iran that began the war in February 2026. His son Mojtaba Khamenei has held the title ever since. Mr. Trump said Iranian officials have been "very, very difficult" to make a deal with. "I mean, we make a deal and then they break the deal the next day," Mr. Trump said. This article originally appeared on CBS News at https://www.cbsnews.com/live-updates/iran-war-us-trump-blockade-strait-of-hormuz-ship-attacks/

item.title: Trump's new order puts companies in the middle of his fight with Congress
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
President Donald Trump walks to speak at a news conference in the James Brady Press Briefing Room of the White House on November 20. - Alex Brandon/AP In a major power play, President Donald Trump is seeking to limit who, how and what Democrats can investigate as they gear up to use their new powers in the next Congress to target his alleged corruption. Key Democratic investigators are pushing back, including against Trump’s executive order Friday that warned businesses that deal with the federal government to coordinate requests for information or communications with the White House. Democratic Rep. Jamie Raskin, incoming head of the House Judiciary Committee, said Sunday that the order “has all the force of an interoffice memo. It’s like saying, ‘We’re closing early before the Thanksgiving holiday.’ It doesn’t mean anything in terms of federal law.” Raskin insisted on CNN’s “State of the Union” that “we have got the Constitution on our side.” Trump ordered companies to comply with executive privilege, the president’s constitutional prerogative, to withhold information from Congress or the courts that could infringe on his office’s capacity to function. He stipulated that firms that refused would risk “the potential termination or cancellation of contracts and the potential debarment or suspension of contractors.” Preemptive exchanges over congressional oversight on multiple fronts offer a taste of the intense Beltway battle sure to unfold next year. The administration has already threatened Democratic investigators with possible prosecution as it resists probes into White House dealings with corporate CEOs, Trump’s architectural projects, including his new ballroom; the business activities of Trump’s family and Cabinet members, and the origins and conduct of the Iran war. The aggressive White House mobilization suggests the president’s claims of executive power will be as expansive in his own defense as they were when he went on offense early in his second administration. A fierce rearguard action was reinforced by the appointment of the combative Stephen Miller as his new chief of staff and House Republicans’ selection of Ohio Rep. Jim Jordan , an adept force of disruption, as their leader. Treacherous days loom for companies that did business with Trump Trump’s order previews a novel confrontation with Democrats over the scope of executive privilege, which is derived from the president’s Article II powers in the Constitution and the separation of powers. The concept seeks to protect the confidentiality of the president’s decision-making. His order on Friday appears — taken to its limits — to imply that any administration business, including with outside contractors, is immune from investigation by Congress. Yet the Supreme Court held in various rulings that the privilege is not absolute and must be weighed against the need for public disclosure. It has stated that the courts, not the president, are the final arbiter in most cases. Any prolonged legal showdown with Congress over the constitutionality of likely blanket privilege claims would mirror a classic Trump strategy in life, business and politics: using the legal system to delay accountability. The sun sets behind the US Capitol building on November 2 in Washington, DC. - Kevin Carter/Getty Images Executive branch power consolidation over recent decades went into overdrive with Trump, who believes there are few limits on his authority and has sometimes been emboldened by a conservative Supreme Court majority with its own expansive view of the presidency. But Trump’s order also points to another significant possibility: that companies who contract with the federal government could find themselves drawn into a bitter fight with two separate and co-equal branches of government. Such firms might risk their immediate business prospects by declining to cooperate with the White House or antagonize Democrats who might — depending on future election results — take the presidency and maintain control of Congress when Trump leaves office in two years. The Trump Justice Department is unlikely to prosecute executives who refuse to comply with congressional subpoenas. But a future administration might take a different view, and top firms could be faced with agonizing political choices. The looming showdown may help define how the public perceives the new House and Senate. Democrats are under pressure to immediately alleviate voters’ cost-of-living woes — a mission that will require the support of a veto-wielding president already balking at their investigative ambitions. But voters also wanted Trump’s bulldozing presidency reined in, and if Democrats have a mandate, it is partly based on concerns about alleged corruption . Political complications to come were reflected in Trump’s comments in a Fox News interview Saturday that he could do “tremendous things” on healthcare and even on immigration with Democratic leaders Sen. Chuck Schumer and Rep. Hakeem Jeffries. But on Sunday, he wrote on Truth Social that Schumer, who faces a leadership challenge from Maryland Sen. Chris Van Hollen, “failed badly” as leader before, “and I have little doubt that he will fail again.” Trump is already pitching a narrative that Democratic probes are overreach amounting to political persecution — a move he used effectively in winning back the White House in 2024, despite being investigated over his attempt to overturn the 2020 election results and his alleged hoarding of classified material. ‘A lawless royal edict’ Raskin insisted on “State of the Union” that Democrats won’t be deterred. “Trump is scrambling to cover up all of the corruption, the kickbacks, the bribery, the insider influence,” the Maryland lawmaker told CNN’s Dana Bash. “They have issued a totally unprecedented and lawless royal edict that private companies not speak to congressional investigators. Every US company, every citizen owes Congress his or her truthful, honest testimony when called to come and testify. And Donald Trump may not like that, but that’s the reality of the situation.” Democrats have already made clear that their investigative sweep will be huge. Sen. Richard Blumenthal has sent letters to multiple companies ahead of a planned inquiry into the funding and construction of the White House ballroom. Rep. Henry Cuellar, top Democrat on the House Appropriations Homeland Security subcommittee, is seeking to investigate contracts awarded by the Department of Homeland Security in the last two years. Democratic Rep. Robert Garcia, incoming chair of the House Oversight Committee, sent letters requiring the preservation of documents to Vice President JD Vance, members of the Trump family, Miller and Attorney General Todd Blanche, among others. Democratic Rep. Jim Himes, in line to run the House Intelligence Committee, last week warned that Congress would withhold government funding for systems developed by Elon Musk’s SpaceX if Musk and the Trump administration refuse to disclose who is responsible for ordering the slowdown of Starshield, Ukraine’s military-grade Starlink satellite service. Democrats may also come calling on law firms that bowed to Trump’s pressure to avoid litigating politically sensitive cases. Democratic Sens.-elect Juliana Stratton of Illinois, Annie Andrews of South Carolina, Peggy Flanagan of Minnesota, James Talarico of Texas, Josh Turek of Iowa and Troy Jackson of Maine at the US Capitol on November 9. - Win McNamee/Getty Images The threat of Democrats using Congress’ funding power to enforce their investigative push is a serious one for both the administration and firms that do billions of dollars’ worth of contracting work for the federal government. The coming months therefore look treacherous for CEOs and firms caught in Washington’s political stew, threatening bottom lines and raising the possibility of reputational damage to corporations that abhor such political complications. Brad Smith, president and vice chairman of Microsoft — which contributed to the White House ballroom project, according to a list of donors provided by the administration — told CBS’ “Face the Nation” on Sunday that “we always have the same philosophy for every administration regardless of which political party it comes from. We partner where we can. We stand apart when we should.” Trump’s executive order comes with teeth. It tasks the Office of Management and Budget with ensuring all contractors comply with its requirements “to enhance efficiency and the protection of Executive information.” And White House Counsel Will Scharf told Garcia this month that the “administration will not be extorted and will not be cowed by unlawful process motivated by animus, pettiness, hatred, or any other unlawful motive to intimidate, penalize, or interfere with the lawful functioning of government.” It’s clear that one key outcome of the midterm elections will be a monumental clash over government power, the Constitution and the Trump’s vision of the presidency that will soon define the contours of the 2028 election. For more CNN news and newsletters create an account at CNN.com This article originally appeared on CNN at https://www.cnn.com/2026/11/23/politics/trump-democrats-investigations-congress

item.title: U.S. intelligence chief warns Americans to brace for more tech outages
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
People should prepare for more technology outages and disruptions to digital services , according to US Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton. In an interview with CNN, Mr Clayton warned that decades-old systems are undergoing urgent upgrades to improve security against emerging cyber threats like autonomous artificial intelligence agents. “The American people should be prepared for a great deal of investment in upgrading our systems; they should be prepared for investment in cyber security , and they should be prepared that any time there is a step change in technology, a step change in both compute and applications, there will be bumps in the road,” Mr Clayton said. “You prepare by knowing that systems are going to be upgraded; they may be interrupted for a period of time and that companies and government are dealing with this on the front foot.” His comments come after a series of major tech failures that caused outages to critical services and digital infrastructure. These have included a global Microsoft outage – which knocked out emails for governments, doctor surgeries and businesses – as well as a communications failure with the US Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) that grounded flights for several hours. Mr Clayton said investment was needed to improve cyber security and protect increasingly sophisticated and exposed networks. “As part of that ongoing upgrade, we are going to have glitches, gaps, interruptions in service," Mr Clayton said. "That ​is ⁠going to happen." Jay Clayton, director of US National Intelligence, speaks during an investor summit in New York City, US, on 20 October, 2026 (Reuters) Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent reiterated the warning on CBS, saying that there could be some issues with updates introduced by banks to protect against AI . “The patches may cause a glitch,” he said. “I think the American people should think of it as a vaccine; your arm may hurt, you may feel a little bad the next day, but it increases your long-term immunity and resiliency.” The White House recently moved to overhaul its cyber security leadership, naming Kirsten Davies as the new National Cyber Director after Sean Cairncross stepped aside. In her new role she will oversee cyber security policy and strategy across the federal government. "Our nation stands in the crossroad of analog, digital, and quantum technologies, our American way of living increasingly interconnected," she wrote in a post on X. "Our opportunity is to dominate the cyber landscape for generations to come… But only if we modernize and drive resilience into the foundations our great nation runs on, as well as build cyber talent for our future." This article originally appeared on The Independent at https://www.independent.co.uk/tech/security/tech-outages-jay-clayton-ai-b3089706.html

item.title: House GOP leadership races against clock as absences continue to derail final agenda
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
House Republicans have just three weeks left in session to advance their legislative priorities before Democrats take control of Congress in January, leaving a narrow window to push through an assortment of unfinished business. At the top of the list is reaching an agreement on a stopgap measure, known as a continuing resolution (CR), or passing all 12 appropriations bills before the Dec. 11 funding deadline to avert a government shutdown. Republicans also face pressure to get the National Defense Authorization Act (NDAA), permitting reform legislation, a farm bill and other items across the finish line. But it won’t be an easy task for Speaker Mike Johnson (R-La.) to wrangle his caucus, especially as he struggles to keep his own members in Washington long enough to get the work done. Attendance problems have already begun disrupting the House floor schedule. GOP leaders postponed a procedural rule vote Wednesday over absences and canceled Friday’s votes altogether. Twenty-one Republicans missed votes on Thursday morning, following 14 absences the previous day. Johnson will need near-unanimous support on any procedural rule if he decides to bring a bill to the floor via regular order, requiring most of his conference to be present as he juggles a razor-thin margin. The House this week took up bills under a fast-track process known as suspension of the rules, which requires a two-thirds majority for passage and is typically reserved for legislation with broad bipartisan support. Because those bills often attract significant Democratic backing, Republicans can afford absences without jeopardizing passage. Johnson called the attendance issue “a great frustration” and told reporters he plans to address it directly with members. He went a step further on Friday and urged his colleagues to show up and vote in a letter posted to the social platform X. “To state the obvious, barring any serious medical issue, we need every Republican to be here to faithfully complete our full two-year term,” he said. House lawmakers left Washington for Thanksgiving recess, leaving them with a little more than a week to address government funding after they return. House Appropriations Committee Chair Tom Cole (R-Okla.) told reporters that he wants to pass 12 appropriations bills and has little appetite for a CR. The three appropriations bills the House has passed so far — funding military construction and the Department of Veterans Affairs, the State Department and agriculture and rural development — represent some of the lowest-hanging fruit. Johnson is sure to face much tougher resistance — both from Democrats and within his party — when the topic shifts to funding other agencies, including the departments of Homeland Security, Defense, and Health and Human Services. Senate Appropriations Committee Chair Susan Collins (R-Maine), meanwhile, released text for all 12 bills negotiated by the upper chamber this month. Republicans on the Senate Appropriations Committee previously told The Hill there are still lots of moving pieces but that the end result is likely going to be some kind of short-term CR. Still, Cole said in a statement that he’s “used to long odds and tight timelines.” “Neither has ever deterred me from doing the work. A lame duck doesn’t have to leave full-year bills dead in the water. … The biggest disservice to the American people would be not to try. I refuse to let any opportunity available pass us by simply because some are already looking at the next Congress while this one still has votes to take,” Cole said. Rep. Nick LaLota (R-N.Y.), who serves on the House Appropriations Committee, told The Hill that “everything should be on the table to pass 12 appropriations bills.” Also on the GOP to-do list is the annual defense policy bill, which is facing an uphill climb in the Senate over its $1.15 trillion request. Senate Democrats blocked the upper chamber’s version of the bill back in July, citing President Trump’s handling of the Iran war. And any NDAA passed by the Senate must be reconciled with the House version, which passed the lower chamber in July. The House is also looking to take up a major bipartisan permitting reform bill that passed the Senate this week. item.title: Trump says Huang is not a national security risk. Why are others so concerned?
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
When news broke Monday that Nvidia had reinstated Jensen Huang as its president and CEO less than two weeks after he resigned amid reports of multiple extramarital affairs — including one with a woman suspected of spying for China — President Trump was quick to reassure the public that "the United States Government has no reason to believe that Jensen's return to NVIDIA poses any risk to National Security." "People say, 'Is it a threat to have him?' No, it's a threat to lose him," Trump told CNBC shortly after the announcement . But not everyone agrees . Before Huang resigned, the Trump administration's own intelligence officials reportedly identified Alice Huang — the Chinese-born leader of a Southeast Asian company called Megaspeed — as a Chinese intelligence asset who kept in touch with Beijing's top spy agency for more than a year while she targeted the Nvidia chief. Why does this matter? Without government authorization, U.S. export controls prohibit Nvidia from selling certain advanced AI microchips — the chips that have powered the artificial intelligence boom — directly to China, America's main AI competitor. But during a period when Jensen and Alice Huang were seen dining and socializing together , Megaspeed wound up buying billions of dollars' worth of those same Nvidia chips. And Megaspeed not only has ties to Beijing . It's actually under federal investigation for potentially smuggling advanced Nvidia semiconductors out of the U.S. and into China. Jensen Huang during the Nvidia GTC global AI conference in San Jose, Calif., on March 17, 2026. Carlos Barria/Reuters As a result, Huang's reinstatement triggered immediate bipartisan backlash. Outgoing Republican Rep. Don Bacon of Nebraska accused Huang of being "compromised and exploited by a Chinese spy" and said "Nvidia should have moved on" without him. "Congress needs to get to the bottom of who approved high end computer chips sales to China," Bacon wrote on social media . "We cannot say we want to win the AI race and then give China our best technology. We need sunlight on who is responsible." Jensen Huang was compromised and exploited by a Chinese spy. Nvidia should have moved on without Huang and ignored the Administration’s inexplicable desire to save Huang. Congress needs to get to the bottom of who approved high end computer chips sales to China. We cannot say we… — Rep. Don Bacon 🇺🇸✈️🏍️⭐️🎖️ (@RepDonBacon) November 23, 2026 Sen. John Cornyn — another retiring Republican lawmaker — questioned Trump's seemingly cavalier attitude toward Huang and China. "No national security risk?" Cornyn posted . "Based on what?" On Monday, Trump took credit for Huang's return, saying he had spoken directly to Nvidia's board. "I convinced them," the president told CNBC . "I made the deal." The U.S. position on chip sales to China has seesawed over the last 18 months. In April 2025, the Trump administration imposed its first major restrictions on AI semiconductor sales outside the U.S., toughening rules created by the Biden administration. But after several meetings between Trump and Huang — who consistently lobbied for letting chip companies do business with China — the administration eventually approved sales of Nvidia's second-most-powerful chip to Beijing. At the same time, " advisers to Trump told him on at least two occasions that U.S. intelligence had uncovered Ms. Huang's links to the Chinese spy agency and that she was in a close relationship with Mr. Huang while he was still running Nvidia," according to the New York Times . But Trump "downplayed the concerns" and refused to intervene because he "regarded Mr. Huang as a valuable ally and Nvidia as essential to the health of the American economy and stock market," U.S. officials with direct knowledge of the briefings told the paper. Meanwhile, After Jensen stepped down, Trump went on to muse about his return and question whether Alice Huang was a Chinese intelligence asset, denying that anyone in his government had ever told him that. "I don't know that she is a spy," the president told reporters last week . "Usually, what happens with that is that any woman coming to the country that's a beautiful woman that comes from China, they say she's a spy." On Sunday, Trump called for Huang's return on social media. The New York Times reported that it came after "several days of maneuvering to provide the company's board with assurances that Mr. Huang was not facing criminal charges and did not pose a national security risk." That maneuvering reportedly included directing Vice President JD Vance, who has close ties to Silicon Valley, to speak with both Huang and Nvidia's board. President Trump and Jensen Huang, CEO of Nvidia, interact during the U.S.-Saudi Investment Forum in Washington, D.C., on Nov. 19, 2025. Evelyn Hockstein/Reuters On Monday, the board announced that it had voted unanimously to reinstate Huang. Trump responded by calling Huang "a Great Patriot and National Treasure" and insisting that "the U.S. Government does not possess evidence that he has engaged in any unlawful conduct." In the same post, Trump added that "NVIDIA should continue its thorough internal investigation of the Company's compliance with U.S. export controls in order to ensure that it is fulfilling its legal obligations and Patriotic Duty to protect U.S. National Security." But an internal probe is unlikely to satisfy Congress. Huang is already set to deliver closed-door testimony on Dec. 1 before three congressional committees led by Republicans — and Democrats have signaled that they will keep investigating the issue when they take control of the House and Senate next year. On Monday, Democratic Sen. Ruben Gallego of Arizona accused Trump of "selling out our national security to keep the stock market high." Another Democrat, Illinois Gov. JB Pritzker, said on social media that "this is the greed and lack of accountability that the country just rejected." "There are serious national security concerns being raised about Jensen Huang that should not be papered over by this administration or the Nvidia board," Pritzker added. The president is a significant investor in Nvidia stock. Last week, the Washington Post reported that by August 2026, Trump held a $13 million to $62 million stake in Nvidia — up from as little as $615,000 at the end of 2024. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent has also accused the commerce department, led by Howard Lutnick, of stalling efforts by the treasury, defense and state departments, as well as the U.S. trade representative, to block chip sales to Megaspeed. "Commerce has the pen," Bessent said on CNBC earlier this month . "You will have to ask them about their internal processes." Lutnick's former firm Cantor Fitzgerald — now led by his sons — has business relationships with Southeast Asian data centers, leading lawmakers on both sides of the aisle to question "whether Lutnick compromised national security to make money for his family," according to the Guardian . Lutnick should have taken "the threats of communist China more seriously," Republican Sen. Tom Cotton of Arkansas told the Wall Street Journal last week . Congressional Democrats have said they plan to investigate Lutnick in 2027. item.title: DOJ admits in court that Trump admin. deported U.S. citizen to Mexico
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
Court filings recount how border patrol agent Robert Gil Jr consulted records from Mexico that listed a Mexican birthplace for Brian Morales. Photograph: Dominic Gwinn/Middle East Images/AFP/Getty Images The Trump administration recently admitted in federal court that it deported a US citizen to Mexico after American authorities incorrectly concluded he was an undocumented immigrant. Attorneys for the US justice department made that admission on Friday while requesting the dismissal of a lawsuit for damages that the deported man – Brian José Morales García of Austin, Texas – has been pursuing against the federal government. Morales García’s case took that turn as the White House has faced bipartisan criticism for the aggressive mass deportation campaign pursued by Donald Trump throughout his second presidency – widely seen as a factor in the electoral battering his Republican party suffered during the 3 November midterms, costing it control of Congress . The Denver-born, Mexico-raised Morales García was riding with his boss to his job as an air-conditioning installation technician on 3 April when they were pulled over by state and local officers near Fredericksburg, Texas. Related: They went out to celebrate at a Memphis bar. Then, ICE descended Morales García was his boss’s passenger and did not have his identification on him. The 25-year-old also told the officers that he had his birth certificate and social security card at home, but they didn’t believe him – so they called immigration agents, who detained Morales García. Court filings recount how Robert Gil Jr, a US Customs and Border Protection agent, consulted records from Mexico that listed a Mexican birthplace for Morales García. Gil Jr also accused Morales García of saying he was born in Mexico and observed that he only spoke in Spanish, according to court records. Morales García was deported on 7 April, with the Trump administration later accusing him in a media statement of being in the country illegally. Morales García’s attorneys sued on 1 May, maintaining that he had falsely said he entered the US illegally and signed papers for a rapid deportation in response to threats of imprisonment by agents. His lawsuit, which seeks an unspecified amount of money, also contended that family and friends tried to deliver documents proving his US citizenship before this deportation. But those efforts were unduly rebuffed, Morales García’s lawsuit said. The Trump administration denied Morales García’s assertions, saying on Friday that he went to Mexico voluntarily and therefore lacked any basis to sue the federal government for damages. Nonetheless, in court filings on Friday, the administration conceded that Morales García “was permitted entry” back into the US on 30 August after it reviewed “information concerning plaintiff’s place of birth”. “Plaintiff is a dual citizen of the United States and Mexico,” Justin Simmons, the US attorney for the western district of Texas, wrote in a court filing first reported by the Texas Tribune . Related: Judge says ICE ‘made a mockery of court orders’ with instant re-arrest policy Americans are not required to carry proof of citizenship when going about their daily business. Lawyers across the US have seen cases such as Morales García’s, which begin after an encounter with local authorities demonstrate how those officials are generally not aware of the nuances of immigration policy. Texas’s public safety department is among many US state and local agencies that collaborate with federal immigration authorities under their 287(g) program . The judge presiding over Morales García’s lawsuit, Robert Lee Pitman, did not immediately rule on the Trump administration’s request on Friday to dismiss the case. The lawsuit also named unspecified local and state Texas law enforcement officers as defendants. An October 2025 report by ProPublica found that immigration agents had detained more than 170 US citizens during the first nine months of Trump’s second presidency. Meanwhile, the media statement incorrectly saying Morales García was in the US illegally is among several related to immigration enforcement under the Trump administration that has unraveled under scrutiny. A Guardian analysis published in July reviewed Trump administration press releases on 26 cases of cars allegedly being used to assault immigration enforcement agents – and nearly all were either disproven or dropped. item.title: '60 Minutes' goes inside community of young people idolizing mass shooters
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
The True Crime Community, known as the TCC by its members, is a growing online community of young people who idolize and romanticize mass shooters. Allizandra Herberhold is a licensed social worker who's spent two years undercover on social media platforms studying the TCC and its members. Herberhold is what's called a "deradicalizer" and has helped 18 kids leave the TCC. She says most kids age out of the dark interest in violence, but some need extra help. "Because I don't speak about them like they're monsters," she said. "I see them as children who are struggling, and they need help." Here are five takeaways from 60 Minutes' report on TCC : TCC is a growing, online subculture Herberhold said most kids inside the TCC are desperate for community, outsiders who are often bullied at school, isolated, and dealing with trouble at home. And like the past mass shooters they idolize, many are battling mental health issues and have a history of self harm. There's also no ideology, according to Katherine Keneally, director of threat prevention at the Institute for Strategic Dialogue. She has been tracking the TCC for the last two years and reports her findings to the FBI and local law enforcement. "It's not a social or political change that they're seeking," Keneally said. "It is violence for violence sake and to gain as much popularity and notoriety in the TCC." She said this online subculture is growing not just here in the U.S., but globally. Keneally estimates that there are thousands of TCC members. Their online content ranges from the romantic — with hearts swirling around past shooters faces — to scary, with some posts egging on members to commit violence or announcing their plans to go shoot up a school. Only a fraction go on to commit acts of violence, but Kenneally's team has identified 12 attacks carried out by TCC members in the U.S., just in the last three years. Seven of them were school shootings. One teen who left the TCC, who 60 Minutes is identifying as Vesper, saw the TCC as a place for kids like him to go. He says he planned an attack on his own school in Australia in 2023. His plot was interrupted when a friend he'd confided in alerted the school. Police determined it was a mental health case, so Vesper was brought to a hospital and put on psychiatric hold. Without TCC, he says he probably would have just killed himself and never conceived of a plot to attack his school. Social media algorithms draw young people into TCC TCC isn't some underground organization found on the hard to reach dark web, Keneally said. TCC material is found on popular social media platforms like Tumblr, Facebook, X, TikTok, Instagram and Roblox. "How kids typically end up in these communities is they're looking at something online. Maybe it's related to school shootings," Keneally said. "The algorithm will then start feeding related content to it." One former member says she remembers seeing TikTok videos suggesting, "You could be the next big one." Keneally views TikTok as the worst platform, alleging its algorithms are perpetuating access to more and more violent content, failing to keep violent videos out of kids' feeds. TikTok says they "prohibit content that promotes violence…and ban the accounts behind it." But 60 Minutes easily found violent TCC content on the platform. "There is a monetary reason that this is happening and there's not really anything that is protecting children at the moment," Keneally said. "And so the responsibility is lying on them to protect themselves, and that's not what it should be." The influence of Columbine on the TCC Megan, who agreed to speak with 60 Minutes anonymously, was 13 when she joined TCC. She was facing struggles at home and battling anxiety and depression. She was first attracted to TCC because of the Columbine shooting. She says she didn't condone the violence, but she related to the shooters, thinking they were similar to her in that they felt isolated, bullied and like they didn't belong. "That pull of, oh, like, the vibe is cool, like, combat boots, and camo, and, and dog tags, and backwards caps," Megan, now 20, said. The Columbine shooters were deeply troubled outcasts who have become central figures in the TCC community. Discussions of the 1999 school shooting continue to this day on social media. There have been nearly 30 TCC-linked attacks worldwide since 2024 Megan has since left TCC, but while she was involved, she says she saw multiple people plan shootings. During her time inside this subculture, she intervened three times to stop potential violence from happening. Since 2024, there have been nearly 30 TCC-linked attacks worldwide. This past May, two TCC members were behind a San Diego mosque shooting, killing three and then shooting themselves, all while recording the carnage. A 16-year-old shooter, also part of TCC, was behind the 2025 shooting at Evergreen High in Colorado. He critically injured two and then took his own life. And one 15-year-old girl posted about violence for more than a year before she opened fire at Abundant Life Christian School in Wisconsin in 2024, killing two before turning the gun on herself. She is now idolized by others on TCC, Keneally said. Her TCC notoriety has inspired copycat attacks around the world. The government and TCC Herberhold travels around the U.S. holding forums to educate law enforcement, parents and schools about signs that a teen is involved in TCC, when to act and where to find members. She says more government help is needed. But the government is moving in the other direction. Last year, the Trump administration cut more than $400 million in grants that supported gun violence prevention programs. When reached on the matter, an administration official said, "The days of funding grossly ineffective programs that have little to no effect on problems they purport to solve are over." The Institute for Strategic Dialogue provides resources for schools, parents and more. This article originally appeared on CBS News at https://www.cbsnews.com/news/tcc-violent-online-subculture-60-minutes/

item.title: Trump tells Army it needs court approval to detonate bomb-making chemicals in Iowa
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
President Donald Trump on Monday said he will defer to a federal appeals court on whether the administration moves ahead with plans to detonate several tons of degraded bomb-making material at an Iowa ammunition plant. The detonation of 68 barrels of lead azide was initially planned for Friday, but the Army has since changed the date three times following an outpouring of public concern about potential health and environmental effects. They had planned for a detonation on Wednesday, saying the weather was most favorable that day. The Army had no immediate comment when asked about the president’s social media post. Environmentalists sued last week in an effort to stop the detonation, winning a stay from the appeals court pending a decision on the validity of an emergency permit approved by the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency that cleared the way for the operation. Trump says he'd blame incoming governor for any ‘death or destruction’ “I feel the proper course is to get rid of this longterm problem but, at the same time, have ordered the Military not to do so until such time as the Eighth Circuit agrees that we can go forward," Trump posted. If incoming Gov.-elect Rob Sand and the court don’t agree, Trump said the administration will have no choice but to not proceed with the planned detonation, adding that he would hold the incoming governor responsible for “any and all death or destruction caused by this very unfortunate, and longterm, situation.” Sand said in a social media post on Sunday that because of previous decisions that have already been made, “No good options exist and the situation is more dangerous and unpredictable than it ever should have been.” He questioned why a contract to remove the explosive risk was canceled, why nothing was done and “why we are rushing to demolition now in late November.” “The safety of Iowans should be the top priority of everyone involved,” he said. “All relevant federal, state and local government resources should be focused on protecting everyone that could be impacted.” Residents left in limbo as they prepare for detonation Some residents near Middletown, where the ammunition plant is located, have been sealing their windows and doors as a precaution to keep out any lead dust that might result from the detonation. Others who live farther away were raising concern on social media about the possible paths that the plume could take depending on shifts in the wind. Officials acknowledge that lead is toxic and have recommended that people stay indoors whenever the detonation happens and clean off outdoor surfaces with water afterwards to limit exposure to any lead particles. Middletown Mayor Rodney Johnson said the detonation must take place “so we can move on with our lives.” “Improper storage and disposal is where things go wrong,” he said on social media. Rachel Rintelmann, an attorney with the environmental group Earthjustice, said Monday she could not yet say what impact Trump’s call for the military to stand down may have on the case. “What I can say is that this post only adds further confusion to a situation that has already caused chaos in the lives of impacted communities,” Rintelmann said. “The people of Iowa deserve better than this.” Army says plans are aimed at avoiding something worse In court filings over the weekend, Army Col. Aaron Teller, a munitions emergency response specialist, explained that less liquid inside the barrels means the solution inside is more susceptible to freezing, which increases the sensitivity of the crystals that have formed around the inside of the rim and underside of the lids. “Even a small amount of friction can break the crystal formation, causing an explosive chain reaction,” he said in his declaration to the court. In March, staff at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant found several dozen barrels of degraded lead azide, which is used in munitions production. Crystallization of the material created an unstable and dangerous situation, prompting the Army to assemble experts in munitions chemistry, engineering and environmental safety to come up with a plan. According to EPA documents, alternatives such as neutralizing and decomposing the drums’ contents with other chemicals were considered. But officials said handling the drums would increase the probability of an accidental, fatal detonation. The environmental groups disagreed, arguing in their court filings that other alternatives were not fully considered. They also criticized officials for not sharing more information with the public. Officials contend that the risk of an uncontrolled explosion is growing, particularly as temperatures drop. They said there is a risk that the chemicals may explode as temperatures are expected to drop below 30 degrees Fahrenheit (-1 Celsius) in the coming days. This article originally appeared on Associated Press at https://www.yahoo.com/news/articles/president-donald-trump-says-ordered-182436842.html

item.title: Medicare for All was once a long shot. Now, parts of it are in Democrats' agenda.
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
WASHINGTON (AP) — What were once long-shot ideas around universal healthcare — championed by Sen. Bernie Sanders' Medicare for All — have suddenly been catapulted to the forefront of the Democratic agenda for the new Congress in January. The party in its first 100 days is planning swift action on legislation to reverse recent Medicaid cuts that threaten to leave millions of people without care and to revive tax breaks that help people who buy insurance through the Affordable Care Act . But it's also becoming clear that the Democrats have far more ambitious healthcare goals as they prepare to take charge on Jan. 3, 2027. Democratic leader Hakeem Jeffries of New York, on track to become House speaker, announced his intentions to take steps toward Medicare for All in a post-midterm election speech that stunned health advocates. He listed proposals to lower the Medicare eligibility age below 65, add dental, vision and hearing aid benefits, and open up healthcare to children as part of the incoming majority's plans — all aspects of Medicare for All. Sanders, a Vermont independent who caucuses with Democrats, unveiled his push for portions of Medicare for All as he takes over the chairmanship of the Senate health committee. And even former President Barack Obama encouraged newly elected Democrats to go beyond the ACA, also known as Obamacare, which was among his signature accomplishments in office. "We got the ACA done, which was wonderful," Obama said, according to a transcript of his remarks to the incoming Democrats at the Capitol. "But I was very explicit at the time. This is a starter home. It is not the answer," he said. "You should push further and get more." After a change election that ousted Republicans in a rebuke of President Donald Trump's party, Democratic leaders are eager to use their incoming wide majorities in the House and the Senate to deliver on their campaign promises, particularly healthcare affordability. The details are still taking shape, and there almost certainly will be pushback from moderate and centrist Democrats who helped win the majorities, especially regarding the costs of any healthcare expansion. But Democratic leaders appear increasingly confident that proposals to expand healthcare are no longer far-flung liberal ideas but are basics that voters who sent them to Washington expect from their government. "It's been an ongoing conversation over the last several months, about how we acknowledge the urgency of the moment on healthcare and that it can't just be going back to restoring what was," said Rep. Pramila Jayapal, D-Wash., who has been in talks with Jeffries about moving the legislation forward. Voters want more government action on healthcare About 6 in 10 voters nationally said the federal government should play a bigger role in helping Americans get healthcare than it does now, according to The AP Voter Poll , a survey of more than 100,000 midterm voters. The same number said they are "very concerned" about the cost of healthcare, according to the survey. Sanders, who has advocated for healthcare essentially since he arrived in Congress more than 30 years ago, is now seen as an elder statesman on the issue for a new generation of lawmakers, including Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, D-N.Y. Jeffries, who had been an early co-sponsor of Medicare for All but backed away once he became House Democratic leader after the 2022 election, recently namechecked Sanders as the "O.G." whose committee will be among those tackling the issue. "We're going to begin very early on in the new Congress by working to reverse the Medicaid cuts and working to extend the Affordable Care Act tax credits," Jeffries said at a post-election conference of Democrats in Denver. "And then we've got to go further to make sure that we don't just fix what's broken but that we build upon what we need to do," he said, as a heckler tried to shout him down. Jeffries went on, "I think we've got to lower the age of eligibility as it relates to Medicare. I think we've got to make sure that we cover hearing, vision and dental, and we got to make sure that every child in America can be able to see a doctor with high-quality, affordable healthcare." Progressives were thrilled. Jeffries had essentially outlined the first year of Medicare for All's multiyear phase-in plan. "We had a sense that he was positively inclined," said Jayapal, who is also a past chair of the Congressional Progressive Caucus, "but he just went ahead and did it." Trump has the power of veto but also a penchant for deals Trump has promised to use the power of the presidential veto to swat back the Democratic agenda. But as Trump takes stock of his final two years in office with Democrats in charge of Congress, he has also indicated the potential for dealmaking with Jeffries and Senate Democratic leader Chuck Schumer. "They're all smart," Trump said about the fellow New Yorkers at a news conference on Friday, his first since the midterm election blowout. "They're going to send things my way, and I'm going to veto them," he said. "But I think after a month or so they're going to send things and I'm going to say, 'I'm going to veto — unless you want to do this and this and this.'" Trump suggested that after years of his own Republican Party's efforts on healthcare — largely attempts to repeal and replace Obamacare — perhaps he could find something better with the Democrats. "There's a real possibility that we'll get a lot of great things done, especially on healthcare," he said. "Now, can it be what they want? No, but it can be a combination of what we all want. And we could end up with great healthcare in our country." Democratic Sen.-elect Abdul El-Sayed of Michigan, who aligns with Sanders on this and other issues, recently posted imagery of "TrumpCare," a golden insurance card, enticing the president to consider a universal healthcare system. Senate could prove an obstacle to their plans With their large House majority , Democrats should be able to quickly pass their initial bills to reverse the Medicaid cuts and restore the ACA tax credits, but the outcome in the Senate is less certain. Democrats will have a 56-seat majority in the 100-member Senate, but most bills in the Senate require a 60-vote threshold to advance over a filibuster, if Republicans try to block the legislation. And Trump's veto threats loom. But healthcare advocates are pushing Democrats to try anyway and see what happens. "Why bother? That's what members of Congress are elected to do — to try and try hard," said Brad Woodhouse, a seasoned strategist and executive director of the advocacy group Protect Our Care, "and if they fail, to try again."
